newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl heads for Far East with business on his mind.
newsitem.headline: Kohl heads for Far East with business on his mind.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl starts a 12-day journey to the Pacific Rim on Tuesday and business will once again be the focus of his talks in five countries.

Kohl, accompanied by a delegation of German business leaders, will use his second trip to the region in the last six months to underline the importance of the Asian-Pacific region to the German and European economies.
Kohl, who has already made 11 trips to the Far East in 14 years as chancellor, will visit Brunei, Australia, New Zealand, Hong Kong and Kazakhstan before returning to Bonn on May 10.
"The entire Asia-Pacific region is becoming more and more important for Europe and Kohl wants to emphasise that with this trip," a senior Kohl adviser said.
Hoping to open new markets for German manufacturers, Kohl is taking about a dozen business leaders with him.
That is far less than the mammoth delegation of 56 captains of industry he brought along on his last trip in the autumn, when he made stops in Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan.

But there is little doubt about Kohl's determination to open new doors for German companies. Germany was the world's second largest exporter in 1996, behind only the United States, with 784 billion marks ($452.9 billion) worth of goods and merchandise sold abroad.
The government and economists have said German firms need to win new markets if they want to stay competitive into the next century.

At the top of Kohl's list on this trip will be the Transrapid, a high-speed magnetic-levitation train developed in Germany that the government hopes will become an export hit, creating jobs in a country where unemployment soared to a six-decade high of more than 12 percent earlier this year.
The government wants to build the Transrapid, whose trains glide on a magnetic cushion at speeds of up to 420 km (260 miles) per hour, over a 300 km track between Hamburg and Berlin.

But the project has come under attack for years from opposition parties and environmental groups who doubt there is sufficient demand for it in densely-populated Germany, which already has an extensive conventional rail network.

There are great hopes in Bonn that Australia could become an important market for the Transrapid, which can cover distances that are often too short for profitable flights and too far to make car or conventional train travel attractive.
The Transrapid could traverse the 300 km between Sydney and Canberra in less than an hour.
Australia, where Kohl will spend five days during the trip, has a population of only 17 million but is seen as an important bridgehead into Asia by many German companies.
Germany exported 5.25 billion marks worth of goods to Australia in 1995 and imported 1.72 billion.
Other German politicians have visited Australia in recent months, including Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt and Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch.

During three days of talks in Sydney and Canberra, Kohl will also try to drum up support in Australia for Germany's Expo 2000 World Fair in Hanover. Australian firms have so far shown little interest in the exhibition.

Kohl was briefly in Australia in 1988, but his trip was cut short by the death of Franz-Josef Strauss, the leader of the Christian Social Union -- the coalition partner of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union.
On his way back, the chancellor will spend a day in Hong Kong. Fifty-two days before the colony's handover to China, Kohl will meet its future leader Tung Chee-hwa.
About 500 German companies have investments in Hong Kong and Kohl is expected to emphasise how important it is for the West that Hong Kong maintain its own economic and social system.
($ = 1.731 German Marks)
